421.title: The night song
421.hook: Sohila means song of praise; its five hymns close the day and close a life
421.carry: a song of joy, for the last night
421.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Kirtan Sohila at night before sleep, often in bed; it is recited when the Guru Granth Sahib is put to rest in many gurdwaras and at the cremation of a Sikh, followed by Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nitnem, the daily rule; your line was both ends held. Today a new stretch begins: the last prayer before sleep.

A lot of homes have a bedtime song. A grandmother humming in the dark. A father singing the same three lines every night, badly, because the baby likes them. The words matter less than the fact that they're the last thing heard before sleep. The day has a lot of voices in it; the night song gets the final word. Sikhs have one too, and it's sung not only at the end of a day.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER HUMMING IN THE DARK.` → `THE LAST THING HEARD BEFORE SLEEP.` → `THE NIGHT SONG GETS THE FINAL WORD.`

segments.voice: It's called Kirtan Sohila, or simply Sohila. Sohila is usually explained as a song of praise, and in old Punjabi it was also a word for joyful songs, the kind sung at weddings. It's short: five shabads, on pages twelve and thirteen of the Guru Granth Sahib, right after Rehras. The first three are by Guru Nanak, the fourth by Guru Ram Das, the fifth by Guru Arjan. The Sikh code of conduct places it at night, before sleep. Some say it in bed with the light off, or play it softly as children fall asleep. And it closes more than a day. In gurdwaras, Kirtan Sohila is recited when the Guru Granth Sahib is put to rest at night. When a Sikh dies, it's recited at the cremation, followed by Ardas. The same five hymns at bedtime and at a funeral. That's not gloomy. Some Sikh teachers describe sleep and death as both a kind of letting go, a handing of yourself back to the One, and the night song meets both with the same calm. The first hymn even speaks of a day fixed in advance, the way a wedding date is written, and friends gathering to bless the one setting out. Over the next two weeks we'll take the five hymns one at a time, sound first, then meaning.
screen: `SOHILA: A SONG OF PRAISE, OF JOY.` · `FIVE SHABADS, THREE GURUS, ANG 12–13.` · `BEFORE SLEEP, AND AT THE CREMATION.` · `SLEEP AND DEATH: HANDED BACK IN CALM.` · then, large: `THE NIGHT SONG.`

segments.voice: Lie back or sit loosely, and let your body grow heavy, as if night has already come. Let one line you've learned on this path be the last thing you hear, anand bhaiaa, or hamree karo haath dai rachhaa, said once, slowly. If you'd like, Kirtan Sohila is in any gutka or recording, and takes only a few minutes.
Sohila. Kirtan Sohila, the Sikh night song: five shabads of praise said before sleep, and recited at the end of a life.
Your line: a song of joy, for the last night. The same calm meets both. Day four hundred twenty-one.

422.title: Hymn 1, sound: jai ghar keerat
422.hook: jai ghar keerat aakheeai kartey kaa hoe beechaaro (Gauri Deepaki M1, ang 12)
422.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Kirtan Sohila at night before sleep, beginning with this hymn of Guru Nanak; in gurdwaras it is sung when the Guru Granth Sahib is closed and laid to rest for the night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sohila, a song of joy for the last night: five hymns that close the day. Today we open the first of the five, sound first.
screen: `SOHILA — A SONG OF JOY, FOR THE LAST NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Every house has a sound. The kettle in the morning. A television murmuring in the next room. Somebody's music through a closed door, the same three songs on repeat. A stranger standing in your hallway for an hour with eyes shut would learn a lot about who lives there. The first hymn of Sohila begins in a house too. Not a temple, not a holy city: any house, named by what is heard inside it.
screen: `EVERY HOUSE HAS A SOUND.` → `WHAT WOULD A STRANGER HEAR?` → `HYMN 1 BEGINS IN A HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here it is, slowly: jai ghar keerat aakheeai, kartey kaa hoe beechaaro. It's Guru Nanak's, in Raag Gauri Deepaki, on Ang 12. Word by word. Jai ghar: in the house where. Keerat: praise. Aakheeai: is spoken. Kartey kaa: of the Creator. Hoe beechaaro: and there is reflection, real thought about the One. So: in the house where the Creator's praise is spoken and reflected on. The next line finishes it: in that house, sing Sohila, and remember the One who made you. Notice the pairing: words said, and words thought about. Then the refrain, the line the hymn keeps returning to. In paraphrase: sing the song of praise of my Fearless One; I would give myself for that song, which brings lasting peace. Fearless is nirbhau, the same word you met in the Mool Mantar at the very start of the path. One more layer. Ghar can mean a building, but in Gurbani it also points inward: the heart, the body, a gathering of people. Some readers hear it both ways. The house where praise is sung might be a gurdwara, a kitchen, or the inside of one tired person at eleven at night. The Guru doesn't say which house. He says what kind.

segments.voice: Say the line once just for its sound: jai ghar keerat aakheeai, kartey kaa hoe beechaaro. Say it again and listen to the room around it, a fridge, traffic, a dog, and let the line sit among those sounds. Then rest in the quiet, and if you pray, whisper it once more.
Keerat, praise: the first of Sohila's five, by Guru Nanak: in the house where the Creator's praise is spoken and reflected on, in that house, sing.
Your line: jai ghar keerat. In the house where praise is sung. That's day four hundred twenty-two.

423.title: Oil at the threshold
423.hook: in the house where praise is sung, friends pour oil at the door for the bride, whose day has come (Gauri Deepaki M1, ang 12)
423.howItsDone: Sikhs recite these verses every night as the close of Kirtan Sohila's first hymn, and Kirtan Sohila is also recited at a Sikh cremation; some Punjabi families still keep the custom of pouring oil at the threshold when a bride or groom arrives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, keerat, praise; your line was jai ghar keerat, in the house where praise is sung. Today, the same hymn's last verses.
screen: `JAI GHAR KEERAT — IN THE HOUSE OF PRAISE.`

segments.voice: A Punjabi wedding doesn't start on the wedding day. It starts weeks before, with a date. Someone fixes the auspicious day, it's written down, letters go out. Then the house fills: cousins, aunties, songs every evening, turmeric, too much food. And at the doorway, a small custom some families still keep: when the bride or groom arrives, a woman of the house pours a little oil on either side of the door, as welcome and blessing. Guru Nanak puts that whole scene at the end of the night song's first hymn.
screen: `THE DATE IS FIXED AND WRITTEN.` → `SONGS EVERY EVENING.` → `OIL POURED AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: The last verses sound like a wedding invitation. In paraphrase: the year and the moment have been written; come, friends, together, pour the oil. Give me your blessings, friends, so that I may meet my Lord. The word for that fixed date is saahaa, the wedding day set in advance. In Gurbani the soul is often pictured as a bride, and God as the beloved she longs to meet. So the bride is the soul, and the wedding is the meeting with the One. Then the hymn turns, gently. In paraphrase: into every house this message is sent; these calls come every day. Remember the One who sends the call, says Nanak; those days are drawing near. Commentators read the wedding here as death, the soul's day to go and meet the Beloved. Read that way, the verse belongs in a night song, and every night becomes a small rehearsal of letting go. But the mood isn't dread. It's a wedding. The friends aren't weeping at the door; they're pouring oil and giving blessings. And the summons isn't sent to one unlucky house. It goes to every house, every day. Nobody is singled out; nobody is skipped. The hymn doesn't ask you to fear the letter. It asks you to be the kind of house where praise is sung when it arrives, with friends at the door when it's your turn.
screen: `THE DATE IS WRITTEN: SAAHAA.` · `THE SOUL AS THE BRIDE.` · `A CALL TO EVERY HOUSE, EVERY DAY.` · `FRIENDS AT THE DOOR WITH BLESSINGS.` · then, large: `THE BRIDE IS CALLED.`

segments.voice: Picture a door you know well, a parent's front door, a friend's apartment, your own, and see the handle, the step, the light. Stand there like one of the friends in the hymn and wish whoever lives inside well: may this house be well. If you pray, say Waheguru softly for the people behind it.
Saahaa, the fixed wedding date: the wedding welcome Guru Nanak places at the end of Sohila's first hymn, where friends bless the bride, the soul, whose day has been written.

424.title: Hymn 2, sound: chhia ghar
424.hook: chhia ghar chhia gur chhia updes (Asa M1, ang 12)
424.howItsDone: This is the second of the five hymns Sikhs recite each night in Kirtan Sohila; in gurdwaras it is recited when the Guru Granth Sahib is put to rest for the night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saahaa, the fixed wedding date; your line was the bride is called. Today, Sohila's second hymn, sound first.

Some lines are built like a drumbeat. You hear the pattern before you understand a word. Chhia ghar. Chhia gur. Chhia updes. Three beats, the same little word starting each one. Even with no Punjabi at all, you can tell something is being counted. It's Sohila's second hymn, Guru Nanak's again, this time in Raag Asa, still on Ang 12. After yesterday's gentle wedding, this one opens short and sharp, like someone tapping a table three times.
screen: `A LINE BUILT LIKE A DRUMBEAT.` → `CHHIA, CHHIA, CHHIA.` → `SOMETHING IS BEING COUNTED.`

segments.voice: The first line: chhia ghar chhia gur chhia updes. Chhia means six. Ghar you met two days ago: a house. Here it means a house of thought, a school. Gur is a teacher. Updes is a teaching, instruction. So: six schools, six teachers, six teachings. Then the second line answers the drumbeat: gur gur eko ves anek. The Guru of those gurus is One; the forms are many. Eko means one, like the Ik of Ik Onkar. Ves is a form, a dress, a guise. Anek means many. In two lines Guru Nanak counts six, and lands on one. Then the refrain. In paraphrase: O Baba, the house in which the Creator's praise is sung, hold on to that house; in it lies your greatness. Hear the echo? Yesterday's hymn began with the house where praise is sung, and today's refrain comes back to the same house. In Sohila the hymns talk to each other, and the word ghar runs through both like a thread. Tomorrow, who the six schools were. Today, just keep the shape: six, six, six, and then one. A count that ends in unity.
screen: `CHHIA: SIX. GHAR: A SCHOOL.` · `SIX TEACHERS, SIX TEACHINGS.` · `GUR GUR EKO: ONE GURU OF GURUS.` · `THE HOUSE OF PRAISE, AGAIN.` · then, large: `CHHIA GHAR.`

segments.voice: Say the line slowly, tapping a finger on each beat: chhia ghar, chhia gur, chhia updes. Then say the answer, gur gur eko ves anek, and let your hand rest flat on that one. Sit and feel the difference between counting and resting; if you pray, say Waheguru as you breathe out.
Updes, a teaching: Sohila's second hymn, by Guru Nanak in Raag Asa, six schools, six teachers, six teachings, and one Guru of gurus in many forms.
Your line: chhia ghar. Six houses, and one Guru behind them. Day four hundred twenty-four.

425.title: Six schools, one Guru
425.hook: six schools, six teachers, six teachings, but one Guru of gurus in many forms (Asa M1, ang 12)
425.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn every night in Kirtan Sohila, and its line about one Guru in many forms is often quoted in Sikh teaching on respect for other paths.

segments.voice: Yesterday, updes, a teaching; your line was chhia ghar: six, six, six, and then one. Today, who the six were.

Picture Guru Nanak's world as a crowded marketplace of ideas. Pandits arguing logic. Yogis with ash-smeared bodies and split ears. Philosophers debating whether the world is real or a kind of dream. Ritual experts measuring every syllable of an ancient chant. Each group had its own house, its own teacher, its own instruction. So many voices: which one do I listen to? Sohila's second hymn walks into that marketplace, and it doesn't pick a stall.
screen: `A MARKETPLACE OF IDEAS.` → `EACH HOUSE, ITS OWN TEACHER.` → `THE HYMN DOESN'T PICK A STALL.`

segments.voice: Chhia ghar, six schools. Many Sikh commentators read these as the six classical schools of Indian philosophy, the darshanas: Nyaya, which studies logic; Vaisheshika, the parts the world is made of; Samkhya and Yoga; Mimamsa, the study of ritual; and Vedanta. Other commentators read the six as six orders of ascetics and their ways of life. Either way, the hymn names the great schools and orders of the Indian world around it. Now the move. It doesn't say five of the six are wrong. It says: gur gur eko, ves anek. The Guru of all these gurus is One, wearing many forms. Tomorrow, the picture it uses to show that: many seasons, one sun. So the six teachers aren't rivals for one prize; they're different garments on the same wearer. That's a striking thing to say in a marketplace where each stall is shouting. It fits the way Sikhs remember Guru Nanak. The janamsakhis, the old stories of his life, show him sitting with yogis, pandits and Sufis, asking questions, answering in song. The point isn't that every teaching is identical. It's that the One is behind them all, and the true teacher is the One. Which brings back the refrain: hold on to the house where the Creator's praise is sung. Whatever door you came in by, that's the house the hymn keeps pointing to.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a real person whose way of praying or living isn't yours, a neighbor, a friend, a grandparent, and something good you've seen in them: patience, generosity, steadiness. Hold that for a few breaths without arguing with it, and let the line sit beside it: one Guru, many forms. If you pray, say Waheguru once, softly.
Six schools. The six houses of thought named in Sohila's second hymn, each with its teacher and teaching, and behind them, the hymn says, one Guru in many forms.

426.title: Many seasons, one sun
426.hook: seconds, hours, days and seasons are many, but the sun is one (Asa M1, ang 12)
426.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this verse each night as the close of Kirtan Sohila's second hymn, and its image of one sun and many seasons is a common illustration in Sikh teaching about the one Creator and many forms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the six schools; your line was one guru, many forms. Today, the picture Guru Nanak uses to show it.

Open the calendar on your phone. Seconds tick into minutes, minutes into hours. There's a Monday and a Thursday, a March and a November, a summer that feels nothing like winter. Some days feel like they belong to a different life. And yet every one of those units is measured by the same thing: the sun coming up, going down, the earth tilting toward it and away. Sohila's second hymn ends on that same observation, made long before anyone had a phone.
screen: `SECONDS, MONDAYS, NOVEMBERS.` → `A CROWD OF DIFFERENT TIMES.` → `ALL MEASURED BY ONE SUN.`

segments.voice: The closing verse is a list of time, from tiny to huge. Visue and chasiaa: the smallest units of the old Indian clock, flickers of a moment. Gharhiaa: the ghari, a slice of the old Indian day. Pahraa: the pahar, one of the watches the day and night were divided into. Thitee: the lunar days. Vaaree: the weekdays. Maahu: the months. Every one of them, the verse says, comes into being. Then the turn: sooraj eko rut anek. The sun is one; the seasons are many. And the last line: Nanak, so many are the Creator's forms. That's the picture behind yesterday's six schools. Nobody calls summer false because winter is real, or makes Thursday compete with Saturday. They're the one sun, seen at different angles. In the same way, the hymn says, the many forms are the play of one Creator. A day of bad news and a day of laughing until it hurts are, in the hymn's picture, lit by the same sun; neither falls outside the One. Some Sikh teachers link this to hukam, the Creator's order running through everything, which came up early on the path. The seasons don't argue about who's in charge. They turn. Winter doesn't apologize for not being summer; it takes its turn under the same light, and then hands the light on.

427.title: Hymn 3, sound: gagan mai thaal
427.hook: gagan mai thaal rav chand deepak bane (Dhanasri M1, ang 13)
427.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn nightly as the third of Kirtan Sohila's five, and in many gurdwaras it is also sung on its own in the evening, often called the Aarti.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was one sun: many seasons, one light. And it's a week's end: Sohila's first two hymns, the house of praise, the bride called, six schools, one sun. Today, hymn three.
screen: `ONE SUN.` · `A WEEK: THE HOUSE, THE BRIDE, THE SIX, THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Lie on your back outside on a clear night and the sky stops being a ceiling. It becomes a bowl, curved over you from edge to edge. Sohila's third hymn starts from that angle. It's Guru Nanak's, in Raag Dhanasri, on Ang 13, and its very first word is gagan, the sky. Its first line is a picture you could almost hold in two hands.
screen: `THE SKY AS A BOWL.` → `IT OPENS ON ONE WORD: SKY.` → `GURU NANAK LOOKS UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening: gagan mai thaal, rav chand deepak bane. Word by word. Gagan: the sky, the whole vault of the heavens. Mai: in, or made of. Thaal: a platter, the round metal tray you'd carry food or offerings on. Rav: the sun; you met it yesterday as sooraj, and rav is another old name for it. Chand: the moon. Deepak: lamps, the little flames set on a tray. Bane: have become. So: the sky is the platter, and the sun and moon have become its lamps. The line keeps going, and we'll open the rest tomorrow, but this much is already a whole picture. Somebody is holding a tray of light. The tray is the sky; the lamps are the two great lights we live by. Notice how the week has built to this. The first hymn began in a house. The second walked through the six schools and ended at the sun. Now the third sets the sun and moon on a platter, like an offering. Sohila keeps widening the frame: a doorway, a marketplace, the calendar, now the whole sky. And the words are plain: gagan, thaal, rav, chand, deepak, each an object you could point to.
screen: `GAGAN: THE SKY.` · `THAAL: A PLATTER OF LIGHT.` · `RAV AND CHAND: SUN AND MOON.` · `DEEPAK: THE LAMPS.` · then, large: `GAGAN MAI THAAL.`

segments.voice: Say the line slowly, one word at a time: gagan, mai, thaal, rav, chand, deepak, bane. Say it again and picture a round tray held up in both hands with two flames on it, then let the tray grow until it's the size of the sky. Rest in that picture, and if you pray, say the line once more.
Gagan, the sky: Sohila's third hymn, by Guru Nanak in Raag Dhanasri, the sky is the platter, and the sun and moon have become its lamps.
Your line: gagan mai thaal. The sky is the platter, the sun and moon its lamps. See you tomorrow.
